reader_explanation.question: Do genes claimed to be targets of NR4A3 fusion proteins show more expression in EMC than a similarly sized arbitrary gene set would, and can that expression establish what the fusion drives?
reader_explanation.approach: The study typed published mechanistic evidence, analysed the small available expression cohorts separately, and calibrated gene-set scores against random sets of the same size. It examined comparator choice and other expression confounds, motif counts, and available surrogate binding/accessibility data.
reader_explanation.main_finding: The pooled set of three fusion-assay genes plus16 native NR4A3 targets reached39% and88% of the two random-set thresholds and exceeded neither; the three genes alone did not meet the four-gene scoring floor. A known EMC expression signature exceeded both thresholds. SEMA3C depended on the comparator, PPARG reused its discovery cohort, and ENO3 survived the expression sensitivity checks but was a pre-designated control rather than an independent discovery.
reader_explanation.main_limitations: The cohorts contain4,6 and10 EMC cases and have heterogeneous comparators. Expression association does not establish fusion causation. Native or paralogue binding in another disease does not measure fusion occupancy in EMC. The available fusion chromatin study measured accessibility in HEK293T cells; the targeted overlap failed the geometry-preserving null. Two nominal occupancy hits did not survive correction; the across-build selection makes the nominal combined calculation indicative. The bounded search also found an unresolved targeted SRA dataset, not a ready fourth whole-transcriptome cohort.
reader_explanation.next_step: Obtain fusion occupancy and a controlled fusion perturbation with RNA readout in a verified EMC model. Distinguish these experiments from deeper native NR4A3 data in another disease, the completed targeted accessibility comparison, and any broader future per-arm reanalysis.

findings.finding: The opening defines random-set calibration well, but subsequent t statistic, null threshold, array platform, native-NR4A3, class A, HEK293T and occupancy terms require specialist reconstruction. The blanket “No class-A gene showed unusual occupancy” also hides the two nominal hits and their failure after correction, explicitly distinguished in §3.11.

additional_abstract_only_changes.before:
Small studies of rare cancers can make many unrelated groups of genes appear unusually active. We asked whether genes proposed to be controlled by NR4A3 fusion proteins in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) stood out from that background.

We compared the proposed group with randomly chosen groups of the same size, separately on each measurement platform. Only three genes had published assays showing an NR4A3 fusion binding DNA. Three was too few for the scoring method, so we grouped them with sixteen targets of the normal NR4A3 protein. This distinction matters: the combined group is not a set of nineteen demonstrated fusion targets.

The combined group did not exceed the random-group threshold on either of the two usable expression-array platforms. A previously published EMC expression signature exceeded both thresholds. Among the three genes, *SEMA3C* changed direction with the comparison tumors. *PPARG*'s strongest result reused the dataset in which it was discovered. *ENO3* remained elevated across the expression checks, but it had been designated as a positive control beforehand, so this is not an independent discovery.

Our bounded search found no measurements of NR4A3-fusion DNA binding in EMC material. Available binding measurements concern other proteins or tissues; two apparently positive comparisons did not survive correction for the number of comparisons. The cohorts are small and their comparison groups differ. These findings show why an attractive expression pattern needs a background comparison. They do not establish which genes the fusion causes to change. Binding and controlled fusion-perturbation experiments in EMC are needed to address that question.
additional_abstract_only_changes.after:
Small studies of rare cancers can make many unrelated groups of genes appear unusually active. We asked whether genes proposed to be controlled by NR4A3 fusion proteins, made when NR4A3 is joined to another gene, in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) stood out from that background.

We compared the proposed group with randomly chosen groups of the same size, separately on each measurement platform. Our literature search identified three genes with assays showing an NR4A3 fusion binding DNA. Three was too few for the scoring method, so we grouped them with sixteen targets of the normal NR4A3 protein. This distinction matters: the combined group is not a set of nineteen demonstrated fusion targets.

The combined group did not exceed the random-group threshold on either of the two usable expression-array platforms. A previously published EMC expression signature exceeded both thresholds. Among the three genes, *SEMA3C* changed direction with the comparison tumors. *PPARG*'s strongest result reused the dataset in which it was discovered. *ENO3* remained elevated across the expression checks, but it had been selected beforehand as a gene expected to test positive, so this is not an independent discovery.

Our bounded search found no measurements of NR4A3-fusion DNA binding in EMC material. Available binding measurements concern other proteins or tissues; two apparently positive comparisons did not survive correction for the number of comparisons. The cohorts are small and their comparison groups differ. These findings show why an attractive expression pattern needs a background comparison. They do not establish which genes the fusion causes to change. Binding and controlled fusion-perturbation experiments in EMC are needed to address that question.

intermediate_review.resolution: The final three abstract-only deltas define fusion, bound the count to this literature search and explain the preselected expected-positive gene.
